mappings.note: Sits on a turning merry-go-round, fixes on a tree and reports which way it seems to move and whether it stays in view: a first-hand observation exercise.
Looks at the Big Dipper, waits two hours and looks again: an observation made over time and recorded.
Covers a friend's head with a thumb and reports the result, the observation on which apparent size rests.
A globe turned west to east under a torch, with the sticker passing through day and night: a working model explained, which is LO-171.
Judges who behaved sensibly at the eclipse, with the answer turning on never looking at the Sun unprotected: safety practice in daily life.
Labels the circles of the eclipse figure as Sun, Moon and Earth, which is completing a labelled diagram.
The small Moon can hide the Sun because it is about four hundred times nearer as well as four hundred times smaller: the phenomenon traced to that ratio.
What to pack for Australia in December: the reversed seasons of the southern hemisphere applied to a real decision.
A lunar eclipse is visible from the whole night side while a total solar eclipse is not: the difference traced to the size of the shadows.
The stem, carrying its own answer, is again the eclipse-visibility question and is mapped on that; the printed answer concerns polar day and night and is reported as a defect.
Fill-in items on stars rising in the east, rotation causing day and night and the total solar eclipse: the phenomena named and described.
True-or-false statements on what causes day and night, on lunar eclipse geometry and on sunrise times: each rests on describing the right phenomenon.
Orion appearing four minutes earlier each night is tied to Earth's motion round the Sun: the shift explained by its cause.
The same four-minute drift accumulated over a year, again traced to the orbit.
Day in India while it is night in the USA, traced to the rotating sphere having only one lit half.
Removing the axial tilt would remove the seasons: the phenomenon tested against its cause.
Shortening shadows are due to Earth's rotation, not the Sun's own travel: a correction of cause.
Stationary trees appear to turn the other way from the merry-go-round: apparent motion traced to relative motion. Not LO-164, since nothing is performed here.
The Sun's east-to-west path follows from the Earth turning west to east: cause behind the daily apparent motion.
Names rotation as spinning about an internal axis: the motion described.
Names rotation as the motion responsible for sunrise and sunset: effect attributed to cause.
Names the axis of rotation through the poles, part of describing how the Earth turns.
The sense of rotation seen from above the North Pole: a detail of the motion.
Twenty-four hours for one rotation. The period belongs to the description of the motion; nothing is measured by the student, so not LO-168.
Explains the day and night cycle from the lit and unlit halves of a turning Earth: the process described.
The Pole Star seems fixed because the axis points almost at it: the appearance traced to its cause.
Rotation against revolution, with their periods and effects: two motions described. LO-162 covers materials and organisms, so it does not apply.
Different constellations through the year follow from the Earth's changing position in its orbit.
Seasons attributed to the axial tilt combined with the orbit: the central cause of the chapter.
Two reasons summer is warmer, more direct rays and longer days, both following from the tilt.
Defines the solar eclipse and its Sun-Moon-Earth alignment: the phenomenon described.
Total against partial solar eclipse, described by how much of the disc is covered.
Why looking at an eclipsed Sun can blind you: a safety warning for real life rather than an account of the phenomenon.
Names a safe way to watch an eclipse, the practical counterpart of the warning.
Defines the lunar eclipse and its Sun-Earth-Moon alignment.
Sunlight is more intense at the equator than at the poles because of the angle at which it strikes a curved Earth: intensity traced to geometry.
Asks what the merry-go-round activity teaches about apparent motion, so the item is anchored on the activity that was carried out.
With no tilt there would be no seasonal shift in sunlight or day length: the cause removed and the consequences traced.
Sydney in June is in winter because the southern hemisphere is then tilted away: the season deduced from the cause.

Explains the solar eclipse with its alignment and the total-and-partial distinction (LO-166) and asks for a diagram (LO-169). The safety line is one sentence of a much longer answer, so LO-173 is not cited.
